books.section: Topic 1.4 Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest
The Early Colonial Era: Spain Colonizes the New World

options.text: It drew thousands of European migrants to settle the high Andes.
options.misconception: Andean mines were worked by Indigenous laborers, not by a flood of European settlers.

options.text: It financed Spain's military and state power, and forced rival crowns to spend in response.
It allowed Spain to abolish the encomienda labor system at once.
options.misconception: The encomienda was curbed by the New Laws of 1542 for moral and political reasons, not by silver revenues.

options.text: It ended European dependence on Asian trade goods and markets.
options.misconception: Silver bought Asian goods; it deepened Europe's trade with Asia rather than ending it.

rationales.general:
1. Follow the silver. Potosi's output flowed into Spain's treasury, and its rivals spent heavily to keep up.
2. Picture the lottery winner. Spain hit the jackpot, the richest mines on earth, and ended up poorer, because the money paid for armies and wars, not farms and workshops.
3. Ask who else felt it. Every European crown competing with Spain had to match it, and when wars cost more than silver, Spain borrowed against the next shipment.
4. Rule out the rest. Silver bought Asian goods, it did not end Asian trade; the encomienda faded for other reasons; the mines ran on Indigenous labor.
Remember: bullion is power when it pays for soldiers, so ask whose army the silver funded.
rationales.B: Potosi's silver paid for Spain's armies and government, and rival crowns spent their own money to match it. That is why the mines mattered beyond the Andes.
rationales.A: The mines were worked by Indigenous laborers under the mit'a draft, not by thousands of European settlers.
rationales.C: The encomienda was curbed by the New Laws of 1542 for moral and political reasons, not by silver revenues.
rationales.D: Silver was used to buy Asian goods, so it deepened Europe's trade with Asia rather than ending it.

stem: After 1545, the silver mines at Potosi produced enormous wealth that flowed into Spanish treasuries and across the world economy. Which broader development best explains the historical significance of Potosi's silver?

stimulus.source_note: Theodor de Bry, engraving of Indigenous workers in the Potosi silver mine, 1590, public domain; the image is a European engraving made by an artist who never visited the Americas.
stimulus.text: The engraving shows Indigenous workers inside the silver mine at Potosi, in the Andes mountains of South America. Workers climb ladders carrying baskets of ore on their backs, while others break rock with tools below. Spanish overseers stand among them. The mine opened in 1545 and became the richest source of silver in the Spanish Empire.
